reception.text: No Arizona or New Mexico paper reported the three monuments in December 1906; the first notice was an Associated Press dispatch from Los Angeles reprinted as filler, with the counties wrong.
reception.source: Arizona Republican and other territorial papers, January 1907

reception.text: A sweep of the digitized territorial press through December 1908 found no opposition from businesses, curio dealers, the railway, ranchers, or homesteaders.
reception.source: Chronicling America, Arizona and New Mexico titles, 1906–1908

legacy.text: Stopping the removal and destruction of irreplaceable objects remains the core job of all three units.

reception.text: El Morro's first local notice came two months late, under the name "Inscription Rock."
New Mexico papers approved of the new monuments and used them as precedent to lobby for more.

legacy.text: In 1917 the Interior Department reported most of the Spanish inscriptions still as plain and legible as the day they were carved.
legacy.source: Interior, General Information Regarding the National Monuments (1917), p. 18

later_actions.text: An act of Congress added Montezuma Well, purchased in 1947.

reception.text: Three months after the withdrawal, a Holbrook paper reported approvingly that Adamana outfitters had hauled about one hundred eastern tourists to and from the petrified forest.

political_impact.text: Taft cut the monument to about 25,626 acres, finding after a geological survey that it reserved far more land than the Antiquities Act's limit allowed.
The Arizona Republican credited the reduction to the reports of the experts; no settler or business pressure is recorded, and Arizona was then asking for better access to the monument.

legacy.text: Congress authorized converting the monument to a national park, with land title as the trigger.
Petrified Forest National Park was established and the national monument disestablished at the same moment.
The Petrified Forest National Park Expansion Act authorized a boundary of roughly 125,000 acres on a willing-seller basis.

today.name: Petrified Forest National Park
today.source: NPS Land Resources Division, listing of acreage, June 30, 2026

later_actions.text: Proclamation 1167 reduced the monument to 40.04 square miles, about 25,626 acres.
Congress authorized establishment of Petrified Forest National Park.
The national park was established and the monument disestablished.
The Petrified Forest National Park Expansion Act authorized a larger boundary of about 125,000 acres.

uncertain: The proclamation map's 60,776.02 acres is about 3,176 acres more than the listed sections total at 640 acres each, and the reason is not known.
